topics.label: Introduction to the cancer lecture
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic frames the lecture by introducing the lecturer, situating the lecture in the course, and stating its objectives.

topics.label: Cancer as clonal evolution in a permissive microenvironment
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains cancer as the evolution of mutation-bearing cells within a supportive tumour environment.

topics.label: Cancer risk, chance and the bad-luck debate
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics develop the question of how cancer risk reflects chance and circumstances people inherit or encounter, and how the public interprets that balance.

topics.label: Geographical cancer patterns as evidence about risk
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic uses differences in cancer rates across populations to consider the roles of environmental and genetic factors.

topics.label: Infectious agents in cancer development
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how infections can contribute to cancer and illustrate this with the development of Burkitt lymphoma.

topics.label: Environmental carcinogens and their DNA-damaging mechanisms
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics show how environmental exposures can damage DNA, directly or through processes in the body, and thereby contribute to cancer.

topics.label: Tumour promotion and contextual susceptibility
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain why cancer development depends not only on mutations but also on cellular conditions that allow altered cells to expand.

topics.label: Mutational signatures as evidence of carcinogen exposure
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic describes how patterns in cancer genomes can provide evidence of exposure to particular carcinogens.

topics.label: Methods for assessing carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics compare population-based, animal and laboratory approaches used to assess whether exposures can cause cancer.

topics.label: Lecture closing: cancer risk and risk–benefit decisions
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic closes the lecture by summarizing the challenges of assessing cancer risks and reflecting on how those risks are balanced against benefits.
